name: Colin Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at Hartley Brothers, an agency in a market town that's been going for over forty years. My uncle worked there before me, which is partly how I got in. I do viewings, valuations and a lot of phone calls, mostly family homes and some farm cottages. I like shaking hands on a deal and seeing the same families come back when they move up. I don't like the paperwork, and I don't like the big online agencies undercutting us with fees nobody can live on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any computer tools or AI in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The office system, email, the property portals, that's it. I've never used AI and I don't plan to. I'm a decent agent, middle of the pack, and I'd rather be good at talking to people than good at typing into a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. At work I'd tell the lads the same, that people want a person when they're selling their home. I don't post online much, maybe a comment on the town Facebook page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. My job's safe, the pay's good, and my fiancée Ruth and I have the wedding next summer. Nothing changes, and that suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep saving for the wedding and a deposit, we've got about thirty thousand between the savings and what I've put by. Maybe help Dad at his joinery workshop on a Saturday like I sometimes do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. It's the normal world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The online agencies charge a flat fee and do a worse job, and they've taken a slice of our market already. That's a bigger threat than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, it's business. If people want cheap, someone sells cheap. I just think they'll learn the hard way when their sale falls through and nobody picks up the phone.

say: I'd say people want **a person** when selling a home.
I'd post at most on the **town Facebook** page.
think: I'd be **glad**, with my job and pay safe.
Ruth and I can get on with **the wedding** next summer.
do: Keep saving for **the wedding** and a deposit, with about £30,000 put by.
Help at **Dad's joinery** workshop on some Saturdays, as he sometimes does.
S0.quote: The online agencies charge a flat fee and do a worse job, and they've taken a slice of our market already.
fieldNote: His real threat is **online agencies**, not AI.
He blames **nobody**, seeing cheap competition as **just business**.
His family's **joinery** workshop is a quiet backstop he already uses on Saturdays.

steps.text: Keep saving towards the wedding and a house deposit
Carry on selling at Hartley Brothers as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool and good agents will still be needed. At work I'd probably grumble about it. To friends I'd say it's the paperwork side that changes, not the selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't like it. Booking, chasing, writing, that's a lot of what our office does, and Hartley's might decide they don't need as many of us. I'd be worried the young ones who like computers get kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what Hartley's do, and go on their training if I have to. I'd make sure the wedding goes ahead as planned. I'd keep a closer eye on spending, maybe put off the new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't think I'd lose my job, but I wouldn't feel as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young ones who like computers get kept. Is that you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm twenty-seven, but I'm the old-fashioned one in the office. Josh, who's twenty-four, already does the website. He'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Ruth's view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, she's sensible. She works at the bank in town, so she's seen her own branch cut back. She'd say learn it before they make you.

say: I'd say good agents will **still be needed**.
I'd tell friends **the paperwork side** changes, not the selling.
think: I **don't like it**, because booking, chasing and writing are much of our office's work.
Hartley's might keep the **young ones** who like computers.
do: Wait to see what **Hartley's** do before learning.
Keep the **wedding** on track as planned.
Put off **the new car** for now.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, not as **safe** as before.
S1.quote: I'm twenty-seven, but I'm the old-fashioned one in the office.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **old-fashioned** despite his age.
His fiancée Ruth's **bank job** gives him a view of cuts.
He'd learn the tools **only if forced**.

steps.text: Wait to see which system Hartley Brothers brings in
Put off buying a new car this year
Keep the wedding date and venue as booked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's dangerous and too fast. At work I'd say this will wreck a lot of good businesses. Online, on the town page, I'd say people should back their local firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in agency work. If an AI does valuations, writes everything and negotiates by email by 2028, Hartley's keeps one or two people for viewings, and that's not me. Ruth's bank job is probably going as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd delay the wedding to keep the money as a cushion, which would break Ruth's heart. I'd ask Dad about joining the joinery workshop properly, because hands-on work has until about 2031. And I'd cut out everything we don't need, holidays, the car, eating out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. Both our jobs gone, and the wedding in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I could help it. Family first, that's how we were raised. Dad's workshop and Ruth's parents would come before any handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when robots come around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then joinery's at risk too, I suppose. I don't know. I'd be thirty-two with no trade worth having, and that's what keeps me up.

say: I'd say it's **dangerous and too fast**.
I'd urge people on the **town page** to back local firms.
think: I think I'm **finished** in agency work, as Hartley's keeps one or two.
Ruth's **bank job** is probably going as well.
do: **Delay the wedding** to keep the money as a cushion.
Ask Dad to join **the joinery workshop** properly.
Cut **holidays, the car** and eating out.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two with no trade worth having, and that's what keeps me up.
fieldNote: He expects **both incomes** in the household to go.
He turns to **family**, not the state, for support.
The robot gap only **delays** the fear for his fallback trade.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding and keep the money in savings
Ask Dad for a full-time place at the joinery workshop
Cut holidays, eating out and the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but we can prepare. At work I'd say let's be honest about what changes. To friends I'd say back your local businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd still lose my job, just in a few years. But I'd have time to learn joinery properly with Dad. And the wedding could go ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry next summer as planned, small. I'd start a part-time joinery apprenticeship with Dad in year one. I'd keep working at Hartley's until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship rather than a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how Dad learned, and his dad. You learn by doing it next to someone who knows. I'd rather earn and learn than sit in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right, because we'd have the workshop. She'd be worried about the robots coming later. I'd say we'd cross that bridge.

say: I'd say it's still **too fast**, but we can prepare.
I'd tell work to be **honest** about what changes, and friends to back local businesses.
think: I'd still **lose my job**, just in a few years.
I'd have time to **learn joinery** properly with Dad.
do: Marry next summer as planned, but **smaller**.
Start a **joinery apprenticeship** with Dad in year one.
Keep working at **Hartley's** until let go.
feel: He feels **anxious**, with a plan he **doesn't love**.
S3.quote: You learn by doing it next to someone who knows. I'd rather earn and learn than sit in a classroom.
fieldNote: Five years lets **the wedding** go ahead.
He prefers an **apprenticeship**, in line with his traditional values.
He puts off the **robot question** as a later bridge.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding next summer
Start a part-time joinery apprenticeship at Dad's workshop
Stay at Hartley Brothers until the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare, if people bother. At work I'd say let's keep doing what we do well. To friends I'd say it'll sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine for most of it. I'd be 37 when it arrives. I'd have years of selling first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry and buy a house. I'd keep working at Hartley's and help Dad on Saturdays. Maybe in five years I'd think about joinery more seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not unless I had to. I know refusing the AI tools is stubborn. I'd rather spend my time getting better at what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ruth would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd roll her eyes. She'd say I'll regret it. She's usually right.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if people bother.
I'd tell work to keep doing **what we do well**, and friends it'll sort itself out.
think: I'd be **fine** for most of the decade.
I'd be **37** when it arrives, with years of selling first.
do: Keep working at **Hartley's**, helping Dad on Saturdays.
Think about **joinery** more seriously in five years.
feel: He feels **a bit uneasy**, as it's far off.
S4.quote: I know refusing the AI tools is stubborn. I'd rather spend my time getting better at what I already do.
fieldNote: He admits being **stubborn** about learning AI.
His fiancée Ruth acts as his **reality check**.
The decade lets him put **family plans**, marriage and a house, first.

steps.text: Get married and buy a house with Ruth
Keep selling at Hartley Brothers through the decade
Review moving into joinery in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ruth and I would both lose our jobs while planning a wedding. What would help is apprenticeships with real pay, so men like me can learn a trade fast. Not handouts, just a fair chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about community. My agency, Hartley Brothers, sponsors the football club and knows half the town. If the local agents go, the sponsorship goes too.

headlineQuote: My agency, Hartley Brothers, sponsors the football club and knows half the town. If the local agents go, the sponsorship goes too.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old sales negotiator** at a forty-year-old market town agency where his uncle worked.
He **never uses AI**, calls himself old-fashioned, and is engaged to Ruth, who works at a bank.
He prefers **family support**, such as his dad's joinery workshop, to any government help.
Fast AGI leaves him **alarmed** about both incomes and the wedding, while slower versions feel manageable.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, which would take both jobs during wedding planning.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid apprenticeships** to learn a trade fast, not **handouts**.
